name: Diffuser curl drying

card.summary: A dryer attachment that spreads airflow to dry curls with less frizz; no trials, and the effect is temporary.
card.note: Heat can dry hair with frequent use.

quick.overview:
Diffuser curl drying uses a wide, softer airflow attachment to dry curly or wavy hair so curls keep their shape. Users say it reduces frizz and adds volume.

No clinical studies were found testing it.
quick.mechanism: The diffuser spreads the dryer's air so hair dries more slowly, at a lower temperature and with less disturbance, according to dryer references.
quick.risks: Heat from dryers can leave hair dry and brittle with heavy use, according to hair-care references.

lead: Diffuser curl drying is the practice of drying hair with a hair-dryer attachment that spreads the airflow, so that curls and waves keep their shape and dry with more definition and volume instead of being blown into frizz. People with naturally curly, wavy, permed or fine hair use it to get a styled, defined head of hair without air-drying for hours. [1][3]

Dryer references describe the diffuser as spreading the air so hair is not blown around while it dries; drying is slower and cooler, which is said to reduce frizz and add volume. [1] Stylists quoted in the press say it helps define curls and covers a larger area than a standard blow-dry, and that technique varies with curl pattern. [3]

For looks, the payoff is hair texture: a clearly formed curl pattern, root lift and less fuzz make hair look fuller and more deliberately styled, which many people treat as part of overall grooming. The effect lasts until the next wash. No clinical trial has tested diffusing for curl definition.

chain: Wide, gentle airflow dries curls without scattering them
Curl pattern stays grouped, with less frizz and more root volume
Defined, fuller-looking hair until the next wash
angle.text: Users apply styling product to wet hair and dry it with the diffuser so curls set in their natural pattern. The visible result is more defined curls and more volume, and it is temporary.

infobox: Curly, wavy, permed, fine or colored hair [1]
Less frizz, added volume, curl definition [1][3]

paras: A hair dryer blows air from a fan over a heating element. Alongside the diffuser, common attachments include a concentrator nozzle that narrows airflow to dry faster and a comb nozzle, which is a concentrator with teeth. [1] Diffusers spread the air over a wider area instead of directing it as a single stream. [1]

Dryers themselves date to 1888, when French stylist Alexandre Godefroy built a seated bonnet dryer for his Paris salon, and handheld household models appeared around 1920. [1] Many modern dryers advertise ceramic elements or ionic operation; the effectiveness of ionic dryers is described as debated. [1]

Styling with dryers is described as forming temporary hydrogen bonds in the hair, which humidity and washing undo. [1] Proponents of diffusing say the gentler airflow dries curls without scattering them, which they associate with less frizz and more volume.

In a Yahoo News piece, celebrity hairstylist Clariss Rubenstein said coily hair benefits from twisting before diffusing so curls do not separate, and suggested combing, scrunching and then diffusing for wavy hair. Trichologist Shab Reslan said the process works on damp hair after product is applied. [3] Both described working in sections rather than moving the diffuser constantly, since constant movement is said to cause frizz and less consistent curls. [3]

Hair-brand and salon sites describe variations such as hover diffusing, which avoids touching the hair, and upside-down diffusing, used for root lift. These are stylist and brand descriptions rather than studied techniques.

General hair-care references note that hair ends overheated by dryers and hot irons can become dry and brittle, and that permed hair should be treated more gently than untreated hair. [2] Reslan advised keeping both speed and heat as low as possible, even though drying takes longer, and said high heat or powerful airflow can disrupt the hair cuticle. [3] Stylists commonly recommend medium or low heat and a heat protectant.

timeline.event: Alexandre Godefroy invents the first hair dryer, a bonnet used in his Paris salon. [1]
